hints: Focus on what stays the same and what changes when you add more gas but keep the temperature constant.
Remember temperature controls the shape and peak position, while amount of gas controls the total area under the curve.
Look for the dotted curve with the peak at the same energy but taller everywhere, so the area is doubled for two moles.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the axes mean**

Think of the curve as a census of energies. The x-axis is energy, E, and the y-axis is how many particles have that energy.

Key rule:
$$\text{area under curve} = \text{total number of particles}$$

**Apply constant temperature**

Temperature T has not changed, so the average energy has not changed. That means the most probable energy, the peak position on the E-axis, must stay exactly where it was.

Any curve that shifts the peak left or right means a temperature change, so we can reject those.

**Apply doubled amount**

We go from one mole to two moles of the same gas. There are now twice as many particles to share out across all energies.

So at every energy value, the number of particles is doubled, the whole curve gets taller, and the total area is doubled:
$$\text{new area} = 2 \times \text{old area}$$

**Pick the matching sketch**

Only one dotted curve keeps the same starting point at the origin, the same peak energy, but is higher at all energies with a larger area. That is the distribution for the added gas.

options.A: Correct. Peak stays at the same energy because T is unchanged, and the curve is higher everywhere because there are twice as many particles. The area under the dotted curve is twice the original, matching two moles.
options.B: Incorrect. The peak has shifted to higher energy and the low-energy part is lower. A shift of the peak to the right means a higher temperature, not more particles at the same temperature.
options.C: Incorrect. The peak has shifted to lower energy and is much sharper. A shift of the peak to the left means a lower temperature, not more particles at the same temperature.
options.D: Incorrect. The peak has shifted to higher energy with a similar height. This is the classic shape for heating the gas to a higher T, where average energy increases but total particle number stays the same.
